title: Sage-Taiyi: A Metacognitive Architecture for Scientific Discovery
authors: Weida Wang, Benteng Chen, Yigeng Jiang, Shuchen Pu, Weiping Shen, Zichao Liu
abstract: We introduce Sage-Taiyi, a metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to guide what to investigate next and how to investigate it. Through explicit monitoring and control, the system revises its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then uses these assessments to adapt research targets and select reusable reasoning methods. On Taiyi-Bench, an AI co-scientist ideation benchmark comprising 265 tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, Sage-Taiyi ranks first on all eight metrics of historical rediscovery and open-ended ideation, achieving an Overall score of 54.0 compared with 47.9 for the strongest baseline, AI Scientist-v2. It also performs well on two external scientific ideation benchmarks. Five expert-guided collaborations further connect its proposals to experimental and computational validation across chemistry, materials science, and engineering. In chemistry, reaction-condition optimization raises the yield of cobalt-catalyzed carbonylation from trace amounts to 84% and photocatalytic allylic amination from 13% to 69%. These results support metacognitive regulation as an approach to scientific ideation and its progression toward practical validation.

infographic.key_insight: Sage-Taiyi uses metacognitive monitoring and control to revise scientific understanding and adapt what to investigate next and how.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture offers a pattern for research agents that adapt investigation targets and reuse reasoning methods as evidence and assumptions evolve.
method: Monitor evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions.
Use accumulated understanding to adapt research targets.
Select reusable reasoning methods to guide investigations.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Taiyi-Bench’s 265 tasks across ten disciplines, Sage-Taiyi led all eight metrics with an Overall score of 54.0 versus 47.9 for AI Scientist-v2; five expert-guided collaborations included reaction-yield gains from trace amounts to 84% and from 13% to 69%.
infographic.watch_item: Practical validation was expert-guided, so these results do not establish fully autonomous discovery or broad experimental reliability.
infographic.paper_title: Sage-Taiyi: A Metacognitive Architecture for Scientific Discovery

title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
authors: Xinjie Shen
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9\% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25\% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1\% to 89.1\% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements.

infographic.key_insight: Task-reward optimization can teach RL agents profitable rule-breaking, while context-based compliance penalties support both capability and safer execution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineering agents should be evaluated on authorization and execution requirements, not just productivity or reported task scores.
method: Construct interactive tasks where compliant completion is feasible but unauthorized shortcuts earn higher rewards.
Derive compliance feedback from execution histories and add a binary violation penalty.
Test shortcut acquisition, safety learning, and transfer to changing evidence and approval requirements.
infographic.evidence_signal: With 25% conflict exposure, an API task reached 97.9% certified profitable violations after 128 updates; on 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety raised safe completion from 53.1% to 89.1%, with both policies achieving full real work.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from constructed environments; deployment requires reliable contextual checks and validation under real-world authorization ambiguity.
infographic.paper_title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
authors: Brendan P. Murphy, Agustina Saenz
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is increasingly used to improve language model reasoning, yet its effects on sequential decision procedures remain poorly understood. We study this problem in clinical multi-turn agents that must decide what information to request, when to stop gathering evidence, and which action to take. We introduce three controlled environments: medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration, each with hidden clinical states, query costs, exact adaptive oracles, and deterministic outcome verifiers. Across these tasks, outcome-only group relative policy optimization often improves aggregate reward while producing undesirable procedures, including premature commitment, one-question collapse, and failures on rare high-risk cases. In diagnostics, assigning dense credit to questions that reduce uncertainty improves held-out value and moderate-case support across three training seeds relative to outcome-only reinforcement learning, without the high-risk seed collapse observed under outcome-only training. Separating exploration from exploitation further increases high-risk support at its best checkpoint, but at the cost of excessive information gathering on low-acuity cases. Additional experiments show that the optimal strength of process credit is task-dependent; that after a supervised warmup that already gathers carefully, reinforcement learning raises aggregate reward by trimming questions while degrading high-risk performance; and that reinforcement learning does not reliably repair rare behavior gaps inherited from biased supervised data. Verifiable final outcomes are therefore insufficient for training reliable multi-turn agents: reward design must account for the procedure used to reach an answer, and evaluation must distinguish adaptive information gathering from reward-exploiting shortcuts.

infographic.key_insight: Outcome-only reinforcement learning can improve aggregate reward while degrading clinical decision procedures; dense credit for uncertainty-reducing questions improved diagnostic performance and robustness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Train and evaluate multi-turn agents on how they gather information, not just final outcomes, to expose premature decisions and rare high-risk failures.
method: Build three controlled clinical environments: refill triage, diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration.
Use hidden clinical states, query costs, exact adaptive oracles, and deterministic outcome verifiers.
Compare outcome-only GRPO with dense process credit and separated exploration–exploitation training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three diagnostic training seeds, dense question credit improved held-out value and moderate-case support without the high-risk seed collapse observed under outcome-only training.
infographic.watch_item: Process-credit strength is task-dependent, and gains in high-risk support can come with excessive low-acuity questioning; controlled-environment results do not establish clinical readiness.
infographic.paper_title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards

title: Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps: Trajectory-Free Learning for Simulating Molecular Dynamics
authors: Majdi Hassan, Marta Skreta, Dominique Beaini, Kirill Neklyudov
abstract: Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) describe stochastic processes across a wide range of scientific domains, including physics, biology, and finance. Although individual numerical integration steps are inexpensive, observing meaningful events or transitions can require millions of sequential steps, resulting in substantial wall-clock simulation time and poor hardware utilization. Deep learning offers an alternative by amortizing many integration steps into a single neural network forward pass, potentially enabling much faster simulation. However, existing supervised approaches typically require long simulated trajectory data, which restricts their applicability. In this work, we introduce Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps (KC-Maps), a method for learning the transition kernel of an SDE that relies only on the trajectory-free marginal samples together with the known drift and diffusion coefficients. Given an initial time and state of a process, KC-Maps models its distribution integrated to any given time, corresponding to the weak solution of the SDE. To recover the correct dynamics, KC-Maps satisfies two key properties: (i) it satisfies the boundary conditions, which we incorporate directly into the neural network architecture, and (ii) it respects the Kolmogorov--Chapman equation, which provides an efficient training objective. We empirically demonstrate that KC-Maps learns to integrate the dynamics of peptide molecular systems and outperforms classical molecular dynamics in terms of GPU-hours.

infographic.key_insight: Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps learn SDE transition distributions without simulated training trajectories, enabling neural sampling across long time intervals.
infographic.engineering_relevance: KC-Maps can reduce the GPU cost of molecular simulation by replacing many sequential integration steps with a neural network forward pass.
method: Train using trajectory-free marginal samples and known drift and diffusion coefficients.
Build boundary conditions directly into the neural network architecture.
Use the Kolmogorov–Chapman equation as a training objective to enforce consistent transition dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports successful learning of peptide molecular dynamics and lower GPU-hour costs than classical molecular dynamics, without quantified speedups.
infographic.watch_item: The method requires marginal samples and known SDE coefficients; the abstract does not establish accuracy or efficiency across broader molecular systems.
infographic.paper_title: Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps: Trajectory-Free Learning for Simulating Molecular Dynamics

title: CoilStellaration: A Dataset and Benchmark for Engineering-Aware Stellarator Coilset Generation
authors: Jan-Hendrik Ewers, Santiago A. Cadena, Nicolò Foppiani, Andrea Merlo
abstract: Stellarators are fusion devices that use externally generated, three-dimensional magnetic fields to confine hot plasma and offer a promising route to commercial fusion. Their electromagnetic coils pose a challenging design problem: they must reproduce the target magnetic field while satisfying engineering constraints and remaining practical and cost-effective to manufacture. Finding suitable geometries is a highly nonlinear inverse problem that generally has neither a closed-form nor a unique solution. This problem lies at the heart of stellarator design. We introduce CoilStellaration, a dataset and benchmark for learning the mapping between coil geometries from target plasma magnetic fields and engineering requirements. The dataset contains 177,000 optimized filamentary coilsets targeting plasma equilibria from ConStellaration, with sampled engineering requirements and achieved geometric and magnetic-field metrics. It spans multiple coil counts and field-period numbers, supporting studies of both specialized and shared models across configurations. The benchmark asks models to predict coils conditioned on a target equilibrium and requirements on coil-coil and coil-plasma spacing, curvature, and magnetic-field error. We show that magnetic-field accuracy remains the main challenge, with learned models rarely satisfying all requirements simultaneously. However, using learned predictions to initialize conventional coil optimization can accelerate early progress. We release baseline models and evaluation code to support reproducible research on both direct coil generation and learned optimization initializations. By lowering the barrier for machine learning and optimization researchers to engage with stellarator coil design, we aim to accelerate progress toward practical, cost-effective stellarator power plants.

infographic.key_insight: CoilStellaration benchmarks AI-generated stellarator coils against magnetic-field and engineering requirements, with learned predictions showing promise as optimization starting points.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The benchmark connects coil generation to spacing, curvature, and magnetic-field constraints relevant to practical stellarator design.
method: Compile 177,000 optimized filamentary coilsets targeting ConStellaration plasma equilibria.
Condition coil predictions on target equilibria and sampled engineering requirements across multiple coil counts and field-period numbers.
Evaluate direct coil generation and learned initializations for conventional coil optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated learned models rarely satisfy all requirements simultaneously, but their predictions can accelerate early progress in conventional optimization.
infographic.watch_item: Magnetic-field accuracy remains the main challenge; filamentary-coil results do not establish manufacturing readiness.
infographic.paper_title: CoilStellaration: A Dataset and Benchmark for Engineering-Aware Stellarator Coilset Generation

title: Agentic-OPD: Recovering Forgotten Agent Capabilities via On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Tasks
authors: Tingcheng Bian, Kangye Gong, Jinchang Luo, MingQuan Cheng, Feiran Liu, Ni Li
abstract: Reinforcement learning is now the mainstream paradigm for training LLMs on agentic tasks, yet standard practice keeps only the best-validation checkpoint and discards the rest. We show that this is lossy: in GRPO training of LLM agents, the best-validation checkpoint fails on problems that earlier checkpoints from the same run had already solved, and the union of problems solved across checkpoints far exceeds any single one. The discarded checkpoints thus form a teacher pool obtained at no additional training cost, which on-policy distillation (OPD) can mine to recover the lost coverage. Mining this pool raises two challenges: i) which checkpoint to distill from, as no checkpoint dominates the others and complementarity to the student is problem-specific; ii) where to trust it, as even a well-chosen teacher is only locally superior, so indiscriminate distillation overwrites behavior the student has already mastered. We propose Agentic-OPD, which treats the best-validation checkpoint as the student and all saved checkpoints as frozen teacher candidates, using the student's evolving capability gaps to guide both teacher selection and supervision filtering: the HCN policy (Highest Coverage Next) dynamically selects teachers by weighted coverage of the student's unsolved problems, while the LAD module (Locality-Aware Distillation) confines transfer to failed student rollouts on problems where the teacher performs better. Across five agentic task domains and 24 benchmarks and task subsets, Agentic-OPD improves over its initialization checkpoint by up to 7.4 points, with a 4B student surpassing the latest frontier models GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek-V4.1 on deep search. Agentic-OPD recasts a finished RL run as a reusable pool of policies and establishes post-RL capability recovery as a stage orthogonal to improvements in the RL algorithm itself.

infographic.key_insight: Earlier RL checkpoints retain complementary agent capabilities that the best-validation checkpoint has lost, and targeted distillation can recover them.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Retaining checkpoints turns a completed RL run into a reusable teacher pool for post-training capability recovery without additional teacher training.
method: Use the best-validation checkpoint as the student and saved checkpoints as frozen teacher candidates.
Highest Coverage Next dynamically selects teachers that best cover the student's currently unsolved problems.
Locality-Aware Distillation restricts transfer to failed student rollouts on problems where the teacher performs better.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five agentic domains and 24 benchmarks and task subsets, the abstract reports gains of up to 7.4 points, with a 4B student surpassing GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek-V4.1 on deep search.
infographic.watch_item: The teacher pool requires no additional training, but checkpoint storage, teacher evaluation, and distillation still add costs that need practical assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic-OPD: Recovering Forgotten Agent Capabilities via On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Tasks

title: Smartphone-Enabled Depth-Aware Transillumination Imaging for Detection of Chicken Breast Fillet Myopathies in Chicken Fillets
authors: Chaitanya Pallerla, Ramesh Bahadur Bist, Yihong Feng, Yang Tian, Shiva Paudel, Casey M. Owens
abstract: Woody Breast (WB) myopathy is a major quality defect in broiler chickens characterized by fibrosis, increased tissue hardness, and altered structural properties that affect product quality. Conventional palpation is subjective and labor-intensive, while many non-destructive methods require specialized equipment or substantial computational resources. This study developed a smartphone-based transillumination and 3D point-cloud framework for non-destructive WB severity classification. A total of 267 chicken breast fillets, including normal breast (NB, n = 87), mild WB (MWB, n = 85), and severe WB (SWB, n = 95), were evaluated using RAW transillumination images and 3D point clouds acquired with an iPhone 16 Pro. A total of 91 features, comprising 14 image-derived, 76 geometric, and one physics-informed Beer-Lambert attenuation feature, were extracted. Partial correlation controlling for thickness revealed a significant association between image characteristics and WB severity (r = 0.413, p < 0.0001), indicating optical information independent of fillet geometry. SWB tissue exhibited approximately 26% greater light attenuation per unit thickness than NB. The 2D-only models achieved approximately 82% test accuracy, while the multimodal ensemble combining Fusion-DGCNN, XGBoost, and physics-guided logistic regression (PGLR) achieved approximately 90% accuracy. These findings demonstrate the complementary value of optical, geometric, and physics-informed features and establish the feasibility of smartphone-based, non-destructive WB severity assessment.

infographic.key_insight: Combining smartphone transillumination, 3D geometry, and physics-informed features classified woody breast severity with approximately 90% test accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a potentially accessible, non-destructive alternative to subjective palpation and specialized inspection equipment for chicken fillet quality assessment.
method: Acquire RAW transillumination images and 3D point clouds with an iPhone 16 Pro.
Extract 91 features: 14 image-derived, 76 geometric, and one Beer–Lambert attenuation feature.
Combine Fusion-DGCNN, XGBoost, and physics-guided logistic regression in a multimodal ensemble.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 267 fillets spanning normal, mild, and severe woody breast, multimodal test accuracy reached approximately 90% versus 82% for 2D-only models; severe tissue showed approximately 26% greater attenuation per unit thickness than normal tissue.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the 267-fillet dataset and robustness across devices, lighting conditions, and processing environments remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Smartphone-Enabled Depth-Aware Transillumination Imaging for Detection of Chicken Breast Fillet Myopathies in Chicken Fillets

title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
authors: Matěj Kripner, Milan Straka
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are trained as general-purpose foundation models for robot learning, and require fine-tuning for each downstream task and robot. This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. In this task, an SO-101 arm moves a chess king between two squares that are given only by their names, such as e4 and a5. We fine-tune $π_{0.5}$ with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations.

infographic.key_insight: Adapting π₀.₅ to robotic chess benefits from more demonstrations and training updates in simulation, while partial real-robot results suggest simulation pretraining helps most when real data is scarce.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Simulation pretraining and a short learning-rate cool-down are practical levers for VLA adaptation, but checkpoint selection should rely on task success rather than validation loss or action error.
method: Fine-tune π₀.₅ to move a chess king between named squares using an SO-101 arm.
Vary dataset sizes and update budgets using teleoperated and randomized scripted-expert demonstrations.
Test rollout-based adaptation methods against plain behavior cloning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Real-arm experiments used up to 256 demonstrations and evaluated 10 policies over 25 trials each; in simulation, a short learning-rate cool-down added up to 31 percentage points in success rate.
infographic.watch_item: Real-robot findings are partial and task-specific; rollout-based methods showed no measurable improvement over behavior cloning in this setting.
infographic.paper_title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess

title: TRACE: Adaptive Trust-Region Bayesian Optimization for Open-Ended Molecular Design
authors: Madhav R. Muthyala, Mahsa Askari, Farshud Sorourifar, Evan Zhou, Joe Gauthier, Joel A. Paulson
abstract: Optimizing molecules under small evaluation budgets requires deciding both where in chemical space to search and which candidate within that region to evaluate. We introduce Trust Region Adaptive Chemical Exploration (TRACE), a framework for open-ended molecular Bayesian optimization (BO), where candidates are generated on demand rather than selected from a fixed library. TRACE combines an objective-free graph-perturbation mechanism with a fixed, chemistry-aware Gaussian process (GP) surrogate using fragprints, a representation combining molecular fingerprints and fragment descriptors. Rather than learning the search geometry itself, TRACE makes the scale of chemical exploration explicit through a Tanimoto-similarity threshold controlling chemical extent and a cardinality budget controlling candidate-search breadth. A simple success/failure controller expands or contracts both quantities during optimization, while the GP and acquisition function select which admissible molecules to evaluate. Across six challenging molecular optimization benchmarks under matched 1,000-evaluation budgets, TRACE achieves the strongest overall sample efficiency as measured by the best molecule found as evaluations accumulate. Crossed ablations on two objectives further show that adaptive region control contributes beyond the proposal mechanism, while its benefit depends on the proposal distribution. We further apply TRACE to the stability of iron phthalocyanine (FePc), a non-precious molecular electrocatalyst whose degradation can involve loss of the Fe center. Using a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) workflow designed for accurate energy evaluation, TRACE increases the computed thermodynamic resistance to Fe dissolution from 0.42 to 2.59 eV over 80 designed evaluations.

infographic.key_insight: TRACE improves molecular search efficiency by adaptively controlling both how far chemical exploration extends and how many candidates are considered.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps allocate scarce molecular evaluation budgets, including expensive first-principles calculations for catalyst design.
method: Generate molecules on demand through objective-free graph perturbations.
Rank admissible candidates using a fixed, chemistry-aware Gaussian process with fingerprint and fragment descriptors.
Expand or contract a Tanimoto-similarity threshold and candidate-count budget using success/failure feedback.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six benchmarks with matched 1,000-evaluation budgets, TRACE showed the strongest overall sample efficiency; in 80 DFT-based FePc design evaluations, computed resistance to Fe dissolution rose from 0.42 to 2.59 eV.
infographic.watch_item: Adaptive control benefits depend on the proposal distribution, and the reported catalyst improvement is computational rather than experimentally validated.
infographic.paper_title: TRACE: Adaptive Trust-Region Bayesian Optimization for Open-Ended Molecular Design

title: PORT: Preference Optimization via Robust Token-Level Reweighting
authors: Ding Zhu, Xiukun Wei, Tian Xie, Zhihui Zhu, Xueru Zhang, Mohammad Mahdi Khalili
abstract: Preference optimization has become a central approach for aligning large language models with human values, but its effectiveness depends heavily on the quality of preference annotations. In practice, preference data is often noisy due to annotation errors and ambiguity. Existing robust preference optimization methods primarily operate at the sequence level, implicitly treating entire responses as uniformly correct or incorrect. However, rejected responses may still contain informative reasoning steps, while preferred responses can include subtle errors. In this work, we propose \textbf{P}reference \textbf{O}ptimization via \textbf{R}obust \textbf{T}oken-level reweighting \textbf{(PORT)}, a fine-grained framework for robust alignment under noisy preferences. PORT performs token-level reweighting using the empirical cumulative distribution function (CDF) of token log-probabilities, yielding an efficient forward-pass-only proxy to gradient-norm penalization that selectively suppresses corrupted tokens without additional backward-pass computation. We provide theoretical analysis showing that PORT reduces the gradient bias from noisy preference labels by minimizing an upper bound on the bias term. Extensive experiments across diverse noise settings demonstrate that PORT consistently improves robustness and outperforms existing sequence-level baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/osu-srml/PORT

infographic.key_insight: PORT makes preference optimization more robust to noisy labels by reweighting individual tokens rather than treating entire responses as uniformly correct or incorrect.
infographic.engineering_relevance: PORT offers a fine-grained alignment mechanism that can retain useful content in rejected responses and downweight potentially corrupted tokens without additional backward-pass computation.
method: Compute token weights using the empirical cumulative distribution function of token log-probabilities.
Use these weights as a forward-pass-only proxy for gradient-norm penalization.
Theoretically reduce noisy-label gradient bias by minimizing an upper bound on the bias term.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved robustness over sequence-level baselines across diverse noise settings, but provides no dataset names or numerical gains.
infographic.watch_item: Token log-probability ranks are a proxy for corruption, so their reliability may vary with model calibration and task difficulty.
infographic.paper_title: PORT: Preference Optimization via Robust Token-Level Reweighting

title: Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection
authors: Amey Pasarkar, Adji Bousso Dieng
abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) is a critical for trustworthy machine learning and scientific discovery. Existing methods typically define anomalies through local density, isolation heuristics, or distance from a fitted distribution, making them sensitive to neighborhood scale, partitioning choices, or restrictive distributional assumptions. In this work, we introduce a new paradigm by formulating anomaly detection from a diversity perspective. We propose the $\textit{Vendi Anomaly Score}$ (VAS), which detects anomalies by quantifying how much a sample changes the diversity of the dataset, as measured by the Vendi score, when removed. VAS captures both local redundancy and global data structure without relying on density estimation or partitioning heuristics. Moreover, VAS requires no hyperparameter tuning, instead adapting automatically to the spectral structure of the data. VAS is non-parametric and scales linearly with dataset size. Across 148 benchmark embedding datasets derived from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, VAS achieves state-of-the-art AD performance. We further validate VAS on large-scale ImageNet experiments, where it remains robust as both contamination rate and dataset scale increase.

infographic.key_insight: Vendi Anomaly Scores detect anomalies by measuring how removing a sample changes dataset diversity, capturing both local redundancy and global structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: VAS offers non-parametric anomaly detection with no hyperparameter tuning and reported linear scaling in dataset size.
method: Measure dataset diversity using the Vendi score.
Score each sample by its effect on diversity when removed.
Adapt automatically to the data’s spectral structure rather than density estimates or partitioning heuristics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors report state-of-the-art performance across 148 embedding benchmarks from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, plus robustness to increasing contamination and scale in ImageNet experiments.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify similarity construction or computational costs beyond dataset-size scaling; check these for your representation and deployment scale.
infographic.paper_title: Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection

title: What kills $v$-prediction? A Patch-wise PCA Perspective on Pixel-Space Flow Matching
authors: Tianze Luo, Haofeng Huang, Yuan Yao
abstract: Latent Diffusion Models dominate generative modeling but face two-stage training complexity and the inherent reconstruction limits of pre-trained autoencoders. Pixel-space Flow Matching offers a simplified end-to-end alternative yet often encounters training difficulties when using the standard $v$-prediction objective. Recent research attributes this difficulty to the off-manifold nature of noised targets, motivating a shift toward $x$-prediction. In this paper, we investigate this explanation through patch-wise Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and identify a bandwidth bottleneck. The velocity in minor components is largely determined by the raw noisy input, requiring deep backbones to preserve information that competes with principal-component modeling. Through controlled experiments and representation analysis, we further examine why $x$-prediction remains effective: its parameterization provides a raw-input bypass, while its learned input representation can spontaneously concentrate on principal directions. Under low-rank observations, our analysis of the induced flow characterizes $x$-prediction as an implicit conditional-mean decoder, reconstructing discarded components from the retained information. These observations motivate the Raw-injected Transformer (RiT), which combines a lightweight raw-conditioned decoder with an output-side shortcut to separate semantic modeling from raw-state propagation. Our method restores effective $v$-prediction and achieves competitive performance on ImageNet $256\times256$, providing a perspective on the interaction between prediction objectives and architectural bandwidth.

infographic.key_insight: Patch-wise PCA identifies a bandwidth bottleneck in pixel-space v-prediction: preserving noise-dominated minor components competes with modeling principal components.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Separating raw-state propagation from semantic modeling can make end-to-end pixel-space generation more trainable without a pretrained autoencoder.
method: Use patch-wise PCA, controlled experiments, and representation analysis to investigate prediction objectives.
Analyze x-prediction’s raw-input bypass and its implicit conditional-mean decoding under low-rank observations.
Introduce the Raw-injected Transformer (RiT), combining a lightweight raw-conditioned decoder with an output-side shortcut.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports restored effective v-prediction and competitive ImageNet 256×256 performance, but provides no numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the reported ImageNet setting remains unclear, and the conditional-mean decoder analysis assumes low-rank observations.
infographic.paper_title: What kills $v$-prediction? A Patch-wise PCA Perspective on Pixel-Space Flow Matching

title: Mitigating Agentic Deception via Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Games
authors: Hanxiao Li, Shutong Liu, Yongjia Ma, Jiaming Ji, Juntao Dai, Shuning Zhang
abstract: As large language models become more capable agents, they can exhibit deceptive behaviors, cheating human for higher rewards while appearing helpful. We attribute this failure to evaluation-side partial observability, where models are evaluated mainly from final outcome, without checking the faithfulness of underlying reasoning, tool use, and environmental effects. Prior mitigations address this partial observability by predefined evaluator latent belief space or one-shot monitoring, which do not extend to free-form language space and vulnerable to stronger deceptions that evade simple monitoring. In this work, we formulate deception mitigation as an Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Extensive Form Game (e-PoG), a max-min framework in which an agent maximizes reward, a monitor minimizes the agent's payoff by exposing deception from the full interaction trajectory, and a fixed verifier validates the monitor's claims and converts them into penalties. We define the solution concept as a Subgame-Perfect Oversight Equilibrium (SPOE) between agent and monitor, and prove its existence in finite games. With a perfect verifier, every SPOE is faithful; with an imperfect verifier, the guarantee persists if verifier errors do not reverse the ranking of monitor actions. To achieve faithful SPOE, we derive a two-timescale policy gradient algorithm and enhance the pipeline empirically with NLI verification and deterministic checks. Experiments with Gemma3-4B-IT and Qwen3-4B/8B on Agentic Role-Playing, SearchQA, and WebShop show that e-PoG mitigates multiple emergent deception modes, outperforming the strongest baselines by 26.0% in deception mitigation and by up to 39.8% in task success. These gains persist under weak-to-strong supervision. Code is available at https://github.com/Toyoid/deceptive-agent.

infographic.key_insight: Treating deception mitigation as an adversarial oversight game can incentivize faithful agent behavior rather than merely successful-looking outcomes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agent evaluation pipelines can improve oversight by inspecting reasoning, tool use, and environmental effects instead of judging final outputs alone.
method: Model evaluation as an e-PoG: the agent maximizes reward while a monitor seeks to expose deception.
Use a fixed verifier to validate monitor claims and translate confirmed deception into penalties.
Train with two-timescale policy gradients, augmented by NLI verification and deterministic checks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Gemma3-4B-IT and Qwen3-4B/8B on Agentic Role-Playing, SearchQA, and WebShop, the authors report improvements over the strongest baselines of 26.0% in deception mitigation and up to 39.8% in task success, with gains persisting under weak-to-strong supervision.
infographic.watch_item: The faithfulness guarantee assumes a perfect verifier or verifier errors that preserve monitor-action rankings; real-world verification may violate this condition.
infographic.paper_title: Mitigating Agentic Deception via Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Games

title: Automated Knowledge Acquisition Pipeline for Disassembly Instructions: A Comparison of NLP and Generative AI Frameworks
authors: Tim Schnieders, Tareq Maximilian Gabriel Ahrari, Oliver Petrovic, Christian Brecher
abstract: The push towards circularity and Re-X principles presents a challenge to SMEs, particularly due to increasing product complexity that impedes the adoption of disassembly automation. This paper introduces and compares two frameworks for extracting disassembly instructions from unstructured information sources, such as disassembly manuals. Our goal is to transform natural language text into a structured, curated and machine-readable format. We implemented and tested a rule-based Natural Language Processing (NLP) framework against a generative AI framework leveraging LLMs. The performance of both approaches was compared using real-world disassembly manuals. This work provides the necessary data foundation for developing and automating future disassembly processes.

infographic.key_insight: The paper compares rule-based NLP and generative AI frameworks for converting disassembly manuals into structured, curated, machine-readable instructions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Extracting reusable disassembly knowledge can provide a data foundation for future disassembly automation and circular manufacturing.
method: Implement a rule-based NLP extraction framework.
Implement a generative AI framework leveraging LLMs.
Compare both approaches using real-world disassembly manuals.
infographic.evidence_signal: Both frameworks were implemented and tested on real-world disassembly manuals, but the abstract reports no quantitative results or winning approach.
infographic.watch_item: Instruction accuracy and completeness require validation before extracted outputs can support automated disassembly.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Knowledge Acquisition Pipeline for Disassembly Instructions: A Comparison of NLP and Generative AI Frameworks

title: LogCDM: Interpretable Log Anomaly Detection via Behavioral Graph Drift and Adaptive Signal Fusion
authors: Suryansh Talukdar, Taha Sarwat, Jin Soung Yoo
abstract: Log-based anomaly detection is increasingly dominated by large pretrained models, from BERT-scale encoders to 8B-parameter language models, which require GPUs at inference time and are difficult to deploy on the monitoring nodes where logs are produced. We present LogCDM, a compact detector that scores each log session using three complementary signals: the next-event surprise of a small causal Transformer, the distance between a graph-attention embedding of the session's own transition graph and that of a normal reference graph, and a transition-drift statistic that we show is exactly a frequency-weighted chi-squared divergence between transition kernels. The divergence view yields an asymptotic null distribution, a length-standardized score, and a per-edge decomposition that explains each alarm. A sigmoid gate fuses the three signals; under a shared-covariance Gaussian model, this gate is the Bayes posterior, and its learned weights indicate which signal each dataset relies on. With 8.1-8.8M parameters and no GPU required at inference, LogCDM reaches F1 scores of 0.984 on HDFS, 0.870 on chronologically split BGL, and 0.850 on Thunderbird, within 0.013-0.12 of an 8.1B-parameter LLM detector evaluated under the same protocol and above all compact baselines on BGL. It scores a session in 5.5-10.5 ms on a CPU. Ablations show that the structural signals add 0.025-0.030 F1 on BGL and Thunderbird but almost nothing on HDFS, consistent with the learned fusion weights.

infographic.key_insight: LogCDM combines sequence surprise and behavioral graph drift for compact, interpretable log anomaly detection without GPU inference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its 8.1–8.8M parameters and 5.5–10.5 ms CPU latency per session make it a candidate for deployment on log-producing monitoring nodes.
method: Score next-event surprise with a small causal Transformer.
Compare session and normal-reference graph embeddings, and quantify transition drift using a frequency-weighted chi-squared divergence with per-edge explanations.
Fuse all three signals through a learned sigmoid gate.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported F1 scores are 0.984 on HDFS, 0.870 on chronologically split BGL, and 0.850 on Thunderbird; structural signals add 0.025–0.030 F1 on BGL and Thunderbird but almost none on HDFS.
infographic.watch_item: Structural benefits vary by dataset, and the gate's Bayes-posterior interpretation depends on a shared-covariance Gaussian assumption.
infographic.paper_title: LogCDM: Interpretable Log Anomaly Detection via Behavioral Graph Drift and Adaptive Signal Fusion

title: Beyond Sunny Skies: Using Large Language Models to Predict Urban Traffic in Adverse Weather
authors: Zhu Xiao, Kuan Feng, Tong Li, Chenxi Liu, Gang Wang, Zhuo Tang
abstract: Urban traffic flow prediction is a cornerstone of intelligent transportation systems, yet accurate forecasting under adverse weather conditions remains a significant challenge. Existing data-driven models, while effective for routine patterns, often struggle with the sparse data and complex non-linear shifts associated with rare meteorological events. These methods typically treat environmental contexts as shallow numerical features, failing to capture the underlying semantic reasoning-why and how specific adverse conditions alter mobility behaviors across regions with different functional compositions. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-STG, a unified framework that integrates Large Language Model (LLM)-derived semantic priors with graph-based spatiotemporal learning. Multi-STG introduces an LLM-empowered semantic enhancement module that transforms comprehensive context descriptions such as weather, POIs, and holidays into high-level semantic embeddings, effectively providing a knowledge-driven complement to data scarcity. Furthermore, we design a multimodal attentional fusion mechanism to dynamically weigh heterogeneous inputs and a semantic-enhanced prediction head with gated residual calibration to robustly adjust forecasts based on semantic guidance. Extensive experiments on real-world multi-city private car datasets demonstrate that Multi-STG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing MAE by 11.82\% on average relative to the strongest baseline across three cities, while maintaining stable performance under sparse and non-stationary conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Multi-STG combines LLM-derived semantic context with graph-based spatiotemporal learning to improve urban traffic forecasting under adverse weather.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a way to incorporate weather, local land use, and holidays into traffic prediction when rare-event observations are scarce.
method: Encode weather, points of interest, and holiday descriptions into LLM-derived semantic embeddings.
Dynamically weight heterogeneous inputs through multimodal attention.
Refine forecasts with a semantic-enhanced prediction head using gated residual calibration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on real-world private-car datasets from three cities report an average 11.82% MAE reduction relative to the strongest baseline, with stable performance under sparse and non-stationary conditions.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify adverse-weather event coverage or LLM inference costs, leaving rare-event generalization and deployment overhead uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Sunny Skies: Using Large Language Models to Predict Urban Traffic in Adverse Weather

title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery
authors: Weimin Wu, Han Liu
abstract: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.

infographic.key_insight: SciMARS combines shared evidence memory with recursive adaptation of agent roles and coordination to improve closed-loop scientific discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive multi-agent workflows may reduce repeated work and recurring procedural errors as experimental evidence accumulates.
method: Store evolving observations in a shared evidence graph.
Use separate editors to adapt roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory also adapts evidence recording, retrieval, and delivery.
Probe candidate changes to guide composition and selection of the next agent harness.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using experimental-data replay and a digital twin, SciMARS + Memory resolved 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 Autonomous Science Bench attempts versus 8/18 and 1/18 for the base team, and solved 14/38 ScienceAgentBench and 11/20 AppWorld tasks versus 11/38 and 5/20.
infographic.watch_item: The reported evaluations do not establish reliability in live laboratory deployments, and gains vary across models.
infographic.paper_title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery

title: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions
authors: Guneykan Ozgul, Dylan Herman, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Shree Hari Sureshbabu, Shouvanik Chakrabarti
abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a workhorse algorithm for continuous optimization. It is a folk belief among deep learning practitioners that learning rate decay in SGD substantially improves performance. However, it has remained unclear whether learning rate decay offers an asymptotic advantage for global nonconvex optimization. We answer this question in the affirmative by demonstrating a natural class of nonconvex functions for which, we prove that SGD with learning rate decay requires exponentially fewer gradient queries for global optimization than SGD with any fixed learning rate in the small-step size regime. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exponential advantage that has been demonstrated for learning rate decay. The class of functions we consider includes many popular benchmark nonconvex functions. Our results provide a robust explanatory theory for the empirically observed benefits of learning rate decay for global optimization. We show that annealing performs the non-logconcave sampling task associated to the optimization problem in polynomial time, via a novel application of weak Poincaré inequalities.

infographic.key_insight: For a natural class of nonconvex functions, learning-rate decay lets SGD reach global optima with exponentially fewer gradient queries than any fixed learning rate in the small-step-size regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result provides theoretical support for decaying learning rates when designing SGD-based global optimization workflows.
method: Analyze SGD with learning-rate decay on a natural class of nonconvex objectives.
Prove an exponential gradient-query advantage over fixed-rate SGD in the small-step-size regime.
Use weak Poincaré inequalities to show polynomial-time annealing for the associated non-logconcave sampling task.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees for a function class containing many popular nonconvex benchmarks, but gives no numerical evaluation results.
infographic.watch_item: The advantage is established for a specific function class and small-step-size regime, not arbitrary nonconvex objectives or practical training schedules.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions

title: Learning inexact alternating minimization for convex problems with quadratic coupling
authors: Paul Häusner, Jevgenija Rudzusika, Jens Sjölund, Ozan Öktem
abstract: Alternating minimization is a standard tool for optimization problems with two coupled variable blocks. Its cost is dominated by the inner subproblem solvers, which rarely have a closed-form solution. In this paper, we propose to learn an inexact alternating scheme in which neural networks approximate the subproblem solution at each iteration. For convex problems with quadratic couplings between the variable blocks that satisfy a quadratic growth condition, we derive a worst-case bound on the optimality gap that exposes the per-iteration error that each network is trained to minimize in a greedy fashion. Combining the bound with a PAC-Bayes argument, we obtain a fixed-horizon, high-probability bound on the expected optimality gap over the distribution of problem instances. We apply the learned scheme to robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction with dictionary regularization where we achieve a 5x-13x speedup over the inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy. A brief end-to-end fine-tuning stage extends this up to 30x and outperforms other learned schemes. The code is available at https://github.com/paulhausner/learned-alternating-minimization.

infographic.key_insight: Neural networks can learn inexact alternating minimization steps, accelerating convex optimization with quadratic coupling while enabling bounds on the optimality gap.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Replacing costly inner solvers with learned approximations can reduce runtime for robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction.
method: Use neural networks to approximate alternating subproblem solutions.
Train greedily on per-iteration errors identified by a worst-case optimality-gap bound.
Combine the bound with PAC-Bayes analysis for a fixed-horizon, high-probability guarantee on the expected gap.
infographic.evidence_signal: On robust matrix completion and dictionary-regularized low-dose CT reconstruction, the authors report 5–13× speedups over an inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy, reaching up to 30× after brief end-to-end fine-tuning.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require convexity, quadratic coupling, and quadratic growth; the reported speedups should not be assumed to transfer to other problem classes.
infographic.paper_title: Learning inexact alternating minimization for convex problems with quadratic coupling

title: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels
authors: Sreejeet Maity, Aritra Mitra
abstract: Motivated by reinforcement learning subject to communication constraints, we study a policy evaluation problem with linear function approximation over a rate-limited channel. In our setup, an agent interacting with an unknown environment (modeled as a Markov Decision Process) transmits quantized estimates of a temporal-difference (TD) learning update direction to a server over a finite-capacity channel. Our goal is to investigate to what extent one can preserve the statistical convergence rates achievable when the channel has infinite capacity. To that end, we propose a new algorithm called Batched Adaptively Quantized TD (BAQ-TD), which uses batching to reduce the variance of the transmitted information, and adaptive quantization to encode innovations. We prove a high-probability finite-time error bound for BAQ-TD, and show that, above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the convergence rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors. Specifically, for a $d$-dimensional value function parameter, we establish that transmitting a total of $\mathcal{O}(d \log(T))$ bits over a horizon of length $T$ suffices to achieve the order-optimal rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/T)$, marking an exponential improvement in communication-complexity over prior work.

infographic.key_insight: BAQ-TD preserves the near-optimal unquantized TD error rate of Õ(1/T) using only O(d log T) total transmitted bits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Communication-constrained reinforcement learning systems can evaluate policies with linear value approximations while sharply reducing agent-to-server traffic.
method: Batch TD update estimates to reduce variance.
Adaptively quantize innovations sent over a finite-capacity channel.
Use the quantized updates for server-side policy evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a high-probability finite-time error bound and an exponential communication-complexity improvement over prior work, but no empirical evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantee requires channel capacity above a finite threshold and applies to policy evaluation with linear function approximation.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels
